set.summary: The Irgun ship Altalena arrived during the truce carrying about 940 volunteers and a large arms cargo. Accounts of the arms talks differ: Lapidot (JVL) writes that Ben-Gurion accepted Begin's request that 20% of the arms go to the Jerusalem Battalion and the two sides deadlocked over the rest, while a World Jewish Congress account says Ben-Gurion rejected the Irgun's demand to retain 20%, insisting there could only be one army. The government ordered the IDF to take the ship, and it was shelled and burned off Tel Aviv on 22 June. Sixteen Irgun fighters and three IDF soldiers were killed; Begin ordered his men not to retaliate, and the Irgun was disbanded into the IDF.

set.summary: The day after the declaration, forces of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon entered the former Mandate territory; Transjordan's Arab Legion operated mainly in areas allotted to the Arab state and in the Jerusalem zone. The IDF/JVL table of military casualties gives Israel's losses in the 1948-49 war as 6,373; historians' estimates of dead among the Arab armies range from about 3,700 to 7,000, and of Palestinian Arab dead (fighters and civilians) from about 3,000 to 13,000.

The only opened figure is JVL's combined c. 10,000 Arab dead. Soldier/civilian split drop: not present in text.

set.summary: Count Folke Bernadotte, the UN mediator, and French observer Colonel André Sérot were shot dead in Jerusalem by members of Lehi, who opposed his proposals to modify the partition borders and internationalise Jerusalem. The killing drew international condemnation; the government cracked down on Lehi, arresting many of its members, and the group disbanded.

set.summary: A UN-brokered four-week truce, with an arms embargo, took effect on 11 June 1948 under mediator Folke Bernadotte. Fighting resumed on 8 July.

set.summary: Ben-Gurion signed the Israel Defense Forces Ordinance, creating a single national army from the Haganah and banning other armed forces; members of the Irgun were absorbed in the following weeks.

set.summary: In the 'Ten Days' between the truces, Operation Dani captured Lydda, Ramle and the airfield. On 12-13 July the remaining inhabitants were expelled toward Arab Legion lines: Morris gives 50,000-60,000 people, the Institute for Palestine Studies about 70,000 including neighbouring villages; many died of thirst and exhaustion on the march. Palestinian sources put those killed inside Lydda at more than 400, including at the Dahmash mosque, and the total including deaths on the march at close to 1,000. An unspecified number of Israeli soldiers were also killed in the capture of Lydda.

set.summary: At the end of October 1948 the IDF launched an offensive that took the Upper Galilee from the Arab Liberation Army under Qawuqji and pushed into southern Lebanon. Morris documents killings of civilians and prisoners at Safsaf, Jish and other villages; the UN Mediator's representative reported that some 25,000 additional refugees had been forced out of Galilee.

set.summary: Between late 1947 and 1949 most Palestinian Arabs in the territory that became Israel fled or were expelled. Estimates range from about 520,000-600,000 (Israeli government figures) through c. 700,000 (Morris) and 711,000 (UN Conciliation Commission) to over 900,000 (some Palestinian researchers). Between 369 (Morris) and 418 (Khalidi) Arab villages were depopulated, most later destroyed or resettled; Israel barred return, and the refugees and their descendants became UNRWA's caseload.

displacement.note: Israeli government est. 520-600k (per Karsh); Morris c. 700k; UNCCP 711k (1950); Abu-Sitta 935k; UNRWA: about 750,000 Palestine refugees when it began operations in 1950

affected_populations.note: Israeli government 520-600k; Morris c.700k; UNCCP 711k; Abu-Sitta 935k.
Displacement of Jewish communities in 1948 is not covered by the sources cited for this event.

set.summary: An immigrant camp (ma'abara) on the site of the depopulated Arab village of al-Khalisa in the Hula Valley, whose early settlers were immigrants from Yemen, became the town of Kiryat Shmona, named for Joseph Trumpeldor and seven others killed at Tel Hai in 1920. Encyclopaedia Judaica dates its foundation as a permanent town to 1950, when the camp was transformed into a permanent residential area; it received local-council status in 1953.

set.summary: About 49,000 Jews (JDC Archives: 48,000), nearly all from Yemen, were flown to Israel from a JDC transit camp in Aden in some 430-450 flights, from December 1948 (mainly from mid-1949) to 19 September 1950. Many arrivals were placed in immigrant camps.

set.summary: The law vested the property of Palestinian Arabs who had left for Arab states or Arab-held parts of Palestine after 29 November 1947 in a Custodian of Absentees' Property, and allowed the Custodian to sell the land to a Development Authority, which could sell it only to the State, the Jewish National Fund or certain other bodies. It also applied to many Arab citizens who had been displaced within Israel ('present absentees'). Palestinian and human-rights groups regard it as the legal basis of large-scale dispossession.

patches.why: drop: quantifier 'most land' removed; verifier's suggested sourced wording used.

set.title: Beit Shemesh founded
set.summary: The town of Beit Shemesh was established in 1950; it was first home to immigrants from Iran, Iraq and Morocco.

set.summary: A joint session of Jordan's parliament approved the annexation of the West Bank and East Jerusalem, whose residents had been given Jordanian citizenship. Only Britain and Pakistan are generally recorded as recognising the annexation; King Abdullah acted over the objections of the Arab League.

set.summary: To house the flood of new immigrants, ma'abarot - immigrant absorption camps - were set up in the 1950s, replacing the less habitable immigrant camps and tent cities. By the end of 1951 roughly 220,000-250,000 people lived in about 125 of them. They began to decline by the mid-1950s and many were transformed into development towns; the last closed in 1963.

set.summary: In 1950 the remaining Arab inhabitants of al-Majdal, about 2,400 according to Haaretz, were moved, most to the Egyptian-held Gaza Strip and some to Lod and Ramle inside Israel. The move was officially presented as voluntary, while historians describe pressure and coercion. The town was resettled by Jewish immigrants and became Ashkelon.

set.summary: After Iraq allowed Jews to emigrate on condition of giving up citizenship and liquidating property, more than 120,000 (by some counts about 130,000) Iraqi Jews were flown to Israel, mostly in 1951 and early 1952, leaving about 6,000 in Iraq. Emigrants could take $140 and 30 kg of luggage.

set.summary: KKL-JNF began draining Lake Hula and its swamps in 1951, completing the work in 1957-58 to create farmland. Malaria control had long been an argument for drainage, though malaria had been largely eliminated by 1949. The valley's Arab villages had been depopulated in 1948. The drainage later caused environmental damage, including sinking soils and harm to Sea of Galilee water quality, leading to partial re-flooding in the 1990s.

set.summary: Israel's population grew from 806,000 in 1948 to 1,578,000 at the end of 1951, mostly through immigration of Holocaust survivors from Europe and of Jews from Arab and Muslim countries, over 300,000 of whom had arrived by the end of 1951 as communities in Iraq, Yemen, Libya and elsewhere left amid hostility and legal pressure. Absorption strained housing, food supplies and the budget.

set.summary: After infiltrators from the West Bank killed a mother and her two children at Yehud, IDF Unit 101 under Ariel Sharon raided the Jordanian-held village of Qibya, blowing up some 45-50 houses and killing 69 villagers by the commonly cited count (UN observers reported 53 at the time), many of them hiding inside. The raid was condemned internationally, including by UN Security Council Resolution 101.

West of the town lay the village of al-Faluja, abandoned in 1948 and destroyed after Operation Yoav. In 1968 about half of its adult population were immigrants from North Africa and a fifth from Eastern Europe, mainly Romania.

set.summary: An Israeli army force attacked an Egyptian military camp near Gaza City in reprisal for fedayeen infiltrations, while another Israeli group ambushed an Egyptian army truck carrying reinforcements south of Gaza. The UN Mixed Armistice Commission found 36 Egyptian military personnel and 2 civilians killed (Egypt's complaint named a seven-year-old boy among the dead) and 29 soldiers and 2 civilians wounded; 8 Israelis were killed. The UN Security Council unanimously condemned the attack in Resolution 106 (29 March 1955).

set.summary: In a libel case brought by the state on behalf of government official Rudolf Kasztner, Judge Benjamin Halevi found that Kasztner, a leader of Hungarian Jewry in 1944, had 'sold his soul to the devil' in negotiating with Eichmann. The ruling shook Mapai before the election. Kasztner was shot in the street in March 1957 and died days later; in January 1958 the Supreme Court largely overturned the verdict.

set.summary: Modern Ashdod was founded at the mouth of Nahal Lachish near the site of the Arab town of Isdud, whose inhabitants had left with retreating Egyptian forces in 1948; its port, an artificial harbour enclosed by breakwaters, opened in 1965. Netivot was founded the same year in the northwestern Negev, mainly by immigrants from Tunisia and Morocco.

set.summary: On the first evening of the Sinai war, Border Police enforcing a curfew brought forward without warning shot dead Arab citizens of Kafr Qasim returning from work; the toll is given as 47-49, including women and children (49 is most often cited), and 13 were wounded. A military court sentenced the convicted officers and policemen to 7-17 years and established that a 'manifestly unlawful order' must be refused. None of the convicted men served a full sentence: the sentences were reduced on appeal, many were pardoned by President Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, and by 1960 all had been released. Brigade commander Issachar Shadmi, tried separately, was fined one hundredth of an Israeli lira.

set.summary: Under the secret Sèvres protocol with Britain and France, Israel invaded Sinai on 29 October 1956; Britain and France issued an ultimatum and attacked the Canal Zone. Israel took Gaza and all of Sinai to Sharm el-Sheikh within days; a ceasefire took effect on 7-8 November under UN General Assembly resolutions. Israeli dead are given as 172 (AP) to 189 (EBSCO); Egyptian dead are estimated at roughly 1,000 to 3,000; British and French dead numbered 82 (AP). During the occupation of the Gaza Strip, UNRWA received lists naming 275 people allegedly killed in Khan Yunis on 3 November and 111 at Rafah camp on 12 November; Israel stated there had been resistance, which refugees denied.

set.summary: Under US pressure and UN General Assembly resolutions 1124 and 1125 of 2 February 1957, Israel announced on 1 March that it would withdraw. It left the Gaza Strip on 6-7 March and Sharm el-Sheikh on 8-12 March 1957. UNEF deployed along the armistice line and at Sharm el-Sheikh, where a UNEF detachment kept the Strait of Tiran under watch; its stationing there required Egyptian consent. The strait stayed open to Israeli shipping until Egypt closed it in May 1967.

set.summary: In response to Fatah attacks launched from the West Bank, the IDF mounted a large daytime raid on the Jordanian-held village of as-Samu, demolishing about 125 houses, the village clinic and a school, and fighting Jordanian troops. One Israeli soldier was killed. The Security Council censured Israel in Resolution 228, and unrest in the West Bank against King Hussein followed.
